title: Crowdfunding: A Democratized Way To Raise Capital
description: This guide teaches crowdfunding fundamentals—how to raise capital by pooling small online contributions from many backers. It serves founders seeking alternatives to traditional financing. Covers key platforms (Kickstarter, Indiegogo, GoFundMe, Patreon, Bonfire, StartEngine), success factors (realistic goals, compelling narratives, strong marketing), and challenges (fulfillment, idea imitation, backer satisfaction). Includes Utah examples like Thread.
body:
In its simplicity, crowdfunding is a way to acquire capital by pooling small contributions from many individuals online, helping innovators turn ideas into market-ready prototypes without relying solely on traditional financing. 

Projects are showcased on platforms where backers may receive rewards, early access, or equity in exchange for varied amounts of capital invested. Key advantages include validating ideas with minimal investment, building an engaged community, and retaining control without traditional investors.

Successful campaigns require realistic goals, compelling narratives, enticing rewards, and strong marketing. Potential challenges include unmet funding goals, fulfillment difficulties, maintaining backer satisfaction, and the risk of idea imitation due to crowdfunding’s public nature.

Many crowdfunding platforms have risen since the method of financing was made popular in the late 2000s, each serving different niches and offering unique amenities and benefits. The following are some of the most utilized sites:

  * [Kickstarter](https://www.kickstarter.com/) has become a popular choice for startups and has funded over 250,000 projects since its inception in 2009. Several successful Utah companies, such as [Thread](https://startup.utah.gov/revolutionizing-wallets-how-thread-wove-personality-into-practicality/), have benefited from its wide network of active pledgers. 

  * [Indiegogo](https://www.indiegogo.com/) allows for flexible funding, giving users the option to continue raising money even after reaching their goal. Its InDemand program bridges crowdfunding and commerce, allowing products to be sold directly upon surpassing funding goals.

  * [GoFundMe](https://www.gofundme.com/) is one of the largest crowdfunding platforms and typically serves charitable causes, such as raising money to recover from medical expenses or widespread disasters. Its personal nature encourages projects to gain donors by telling a story.

  * [Patreon](https://www.patreon.com/) uses a subscription-based model to promote and support artists, writers, musicians, and others in similar fields. Its emphasis on recurring support and fan engagement empowers creators to turn their passion projects into sustainable careers.

  * [Bonfire](https://www.bonfire.com/) differs from other crowdfunding platforms by focusing on creating custom merchandise, such as T-shirts and other apparel, to help raise funds for projects, causes, or personal needs.

  * [StartEngine](https://www.startengine.com/) is an equity crowdfunding platform, which means it takes a different approach from other crowdfunding sites by trading capital for a direct financial stake in the product or business. 

There are dozens of crowdfunding platforms, each leveraging the power of the crowd to help support innovators and their ideas. Through these diverse sources of acquiring capital, individuals can bypass traditional funding barriers, validate their concepts, and build a community around their projects.

title: Explore Grants to Propel Your Business Forward
description: This guide teaches small business owners how to find and secure grants as debt-free funding. It covers identifying grant purposes (R&D, expansion), searching by business classification (minority-owned, women-owned, veteran-owned), and connecting with government, private, and local grant sources. Includes resources like SBIR.gov, Grants.gov, and industry-specific organizations. Emphasizes time investment, application preparation, and record-keeping post-award.
body:
Grants can be a key strategy for small businesses to secure funding without taking on debt. There are many grant opportunities, but finding them can be a significant challenge.

Although the idea of “free money” sounds appealing, the investment is often time and effort. Ask whether you can make these a priority:

  * Dedicate time to finding grants aligning with your business goals and stage of development.
  * Prepare for the application process. Some can be completed in a day, while others require months of preparation.
  * Upon winning, keep meticulous records of money spent and milestones met.

If you’re prepared to prioritize these items, consider these methods for finding grants.

**Consider the grant’s purpose**

When pursuing grants, start by identifying your business’s goals and needs. Are you looking to fund research or expand your operations? Government initiatives, like the [Small Business Innovation Research](https://startup.utah.gov/sbir-and-sttr-programs-grant-funding-to-innovative-deep-tech-products/) [(SBIR)](https://startup.utah.gov/sbir-and-sttr-programs-grant-funding-to-innovative-deep-tech-products/) program, help to fund research and development of innovative early-stage projects. You can search [SBIR.gov](http://sbir.gov/) to see the specific technologies agencies are seeking. Other resources for federal grants include websites like [Grants.gov](http://grants.gov/) and[ SBA.gov](http://sba.gov/).

If you own a business in rural Utah or serve a specific industry, you can explore open grants with the[ Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity](https://business.utah.gov/grants/) or connect with one of Utah’s many industry-specific organizations.

**Search by business classification**

Grants can generally be divided into two categories: government and private. However, further distinctions can help narrow your search. Is your business [minority-owned](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/grow-your-business/minority-owned-businesses),[ women-owned](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/grow-your-business/women-owned-businesses), or[ veteran-owned](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/grow-your-business/veteran-owned-businesses)? Federal programs like the [Minority Business Development Agency](https://www.mbda.gov/financial-resources/grants),[ Office of Women’s Business Ownership](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/grow-your-business/women-owned-businesses), or [Veterans Business Outreach Center](https://www.sba.gov/local-assistance/resource-partners/veterans-business-outreach-center-vboc-program) offer grants or can connect you with other groups that do.

**Connect with private and local organizations**

Another option is to seek out private grants. Larger corporations such as the [FedEx Small Business Grant](https://www.fedex.com/en-us/small-business/grant-contest.html) or the [Visa Everywhere Initiative](https://usa.visa.com/visa-everywhere/everywhere-initiative.html) support companies making a difference in their industries. Local community foundations or nonprofit organizations may also provide grants driving regional economic development. Take the time to research and build connections with local organizations.

Remember to be vigilant in avoiding scams when searching for grants. Be wary of applications requiring a fee or private solicitations via social media. It may be worthwhile to seek advice from your local [Small Business Development Center](https://utahsbdc.org/resources/) or other trusted advisors before proceeding.

Grants can be a powerful resource for small businesses. With careful planning and follow-through, grants can be a tool to fuel your business growth.

The information in this article is current as of the publishing date and is intended for informational purposes only. This article does not, and is not intended to, constitute legal, tax, or business advice. Any resources and organizations mentioned, unless an entity of or a partner of the state of Utah, are not formally endorsed by the Startup State Initiative or state of Utah.

title: Pitch Competitions: Providing Funding, Feedback, and Validation for Utah Startups
description: This guide teaches Utah entrepreneurs how pitch competitions provide non-dilutive funding, investor feedback, and business validation. It profiles six major competitions across the state—from Get Started ($500) to Utah Tech Week ($250K)—with eligibility, prize structures, and milestones. Ideal for early-stage founders seeking capital without equity loss and visibility in Utah's robust startup ecosystem.
body:
Funding is essential to building and sustaining a business, but many sources require ongoing payments or giving up equity. Pitch competitions offer a unique alternative — entrepreneurs present their ideas to judges or investors, allowing them to gain visibility and valuable feedback as well as capital. 

Due to Utah’s robust entrepreneurial ecosystem, dozens of pitch competitions are held across the state year-round. Some offer upwards of hundreds of thousands of dollars, and others simply strive to steer entrepreneurs and their startups in the right direction.

The [Get Started: Business Idea Challenge](https://startup.utah.gov/turn-ideas-into-action-with-the-startup-states-new-funding-challenge/) is a pitch competition hosted by the Startup State Initiative in partnership with the [Lassonde Entrepreneur Institute](https://startup.utah.gov/how-the-lassonde-entrepreneur-institute-is-driving-student-innovation-in-utah/). Earning up to $500 of non-equity funding for any type of business idea, winners are to complete milestones that will progress their startups. Awardees also receive recognition by being featured on social media and the Startup State Initiative’s newsroom.

The [State Bank Business Challenge](https://oneutahsummit.utah.gov/sbbc/) is held during the [One Utah Summit](https://oneutahsummit.utah.gov/), an annual event where business owners and state leaders connect. The pitch competition is intended to identify and support early-stage businesses with high potential, offering $50,000 to winners in 2025. 

[Get Seeded](https://lassonde.utah.edu/getseeded/), a program run by the [Lassonde Entrepreneur Institute](https://lassonde.utah.edu/), gives students a chance to pitch their business ideas and gain early funding and traction. It offers two types of microgrants, which encourage students to complete 30- to 90-day milestones. One grant awards up to $500, and the other offers $500 to $1,500.

[Utah Tech Week](https://www.utahtechweek.com/) is an annual gathering where startups, investors, and technology leaders connect over several days of events. A highlight is the pitch competition, where companies have been known to secure up to $250,000 in funding. Those in the audience also have a chance to participate in an open mic flash pitch session to promote their business.

The annual [Rise & Thrive Business Pitch Competition](https://www.uintahspeedpitch.com/), sponsored by the Uintah County Economic Development and the Vernal Innovation Hub, is an example of a more local-based competition. In addition to funding ranging from $4,000 to $12,000, the top three contestants receive full-ride scholarships to the Uintah Basin Technical College for a program of their choice. 

In a business-rich environment like Utah, these are only some of the pitch competitions the state has to offer. As with any funding source, it’s important to research before applying and ensure eligibility and deadlines are met. For more information, check out the Startup State Initiative’s [event page](https://startup.utah.gov/events/list/?tribe_eventcategory%5B0%5D=343).

title: Prepare Your Utah Business to Apply for up to $200K in Project-Based Funding
description: This guide teaches Utah businesses how to prepare for the Economic Assistance Grant, a project-based funding opportunity offering up to $200K from the Governor's Office of Economic Opportunity. It covers eligibility requirements, three funding tiers ($50K–$200K), application deadlines, and what reviewers expect: clear metrics, strong budgets, and 18-month project completion plans. Ideal for for-profit and nonprofit organizations in targeted industries seeking growth capital.
body:
With summer ending and fall steadily approaching, [grant season](https://startup.utah.gov/explore-grants-to-propel-your-business-forward/) is gearing up, providing many Utah businesses with a chance to take a big step forward. The [Economic Assistance Grant](https://business.utah.gov/grants/economic-assistance-grant/), issued by the Utah Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity, is one such offering — drawing from a $4.5 million fund to provide one-time, project-based financing. 

The grant, which is taking applications from Sept. 1 to Sept. 15, is designed to support projects that enhance Utah’s economic landscape, focusing on industry, education, infrastructure, and community development. It’s open to both for-profit and nonprofit organizations, so long as they’re based in Utah and registered in good standing with the Utah Division of Corporations and Commercial Code.

“The Economic Assistance Grant offers a transformative opportunity for businesses to drive growth and innovation in Utah,” said Jim Grover, managing director of economic growth at GOEO. “We invite Utah companies focused on developing the state’s [targeted industries](https://business.utah.gov/targeted-industries/) to apply.”

To ensure fair competition, grant applications are divided into three funding tiers: Tier 1 for up to $50,000; Tier 2 between $50,000 and $100,000; and Tier 3 greater than $100,000, with a maximum award of $200,000.

In the past, the grant has funded diverse projects that have gone on to have a notable impact on the state’s economy and ecosystem. [Wasatch Biolabs](https://www.wasatchbiolabs.com/), a Heber City biotechnology company, was awarded an Economic Assistance grant in the fall of 2023, which allowed the company to upgrade its DNA and RNA sequencing capabilities. The result: faster diagnostics, improved patient outcomes, and an expanded role in Utah’s growing biotech sector.

Opportunities like the EAG are about more than dollars — they’re about momentum. Businesses interested in applying should be prepared to present clear metrics, strong budgets, and a plan that can be completed within 18 months of receiving the award.

Visit [GOEO’s website](https://business.utah.gov/grants/economic-assistance-grant/) for more information about the Economic Assistance Grant. Looking to further support your small business in Utah? See what type of [funding](https://startup.utah.gov/small-business-funding-finding-the-best-option-for-your-needs/) is right for your business, and check out the Startup State Initiative’s [resources page](https://startup.utah.gov/resources/) to move your business forward.

title: Small Business Funding: Finding the Best Option for Your Needs
description: This guide teaches entrepreneurs how to identify and secure the best funding source for their startup by comparing grants, government programs, crowdfunding, venture capital, angel investors, and bootstrapping. It serves founders at all stages seeking to move from idea to revenue, with concrete Utah-based resources like SBIR/STTR programs, APEX Accelerator, angel groups, and crowdfunding platforms. Emphasizes matching funding type to business model and often combining multiple sources.
body:
Funding is crucial to move any business or product from the idea stage to revenue. While there are many ways to acquire financing, the best option depends on the entrepreneur’s needs and business model.

### **Grants**

[Grants](https://startup.utah.gov/explore-grants-to-propel-your-business-forward/) can be a valuable way for small businesses to secure funding without taking on debt or giving up equity. Consider the grant’s purpose to ensure it aligns with your business goals, as many grants support specific industries, innovations, or community initiatives. Search by business classification since some opportunities are designed for minority-owned, women-owned, or rural businesses. Connect with private and local organizations that offer funding, as well as state and federal government programs that provide grants to businesses driving industry advancements and regional growth.

### **Government Funding**

While government funding is often associated with grants, state and federal programs offer various financial assistance options for those doing business in Utah.

  * The****[**Utah Innovation Center**](https://business.utah.gov/innovation/) helps startups apply for federal [Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR)](https://startup.utah.gov/sbir-and-sttr-programs-grant-funding-to-innovative-deep-tech-products/) funding for innovative products, providing about $4 billion annually. The center also offers microgrants of $3,000–$5,000 through the [Utah Technology Innovation Funding](https://business.utah.gov/innovation/utif/) program to first-time Phase I applicants.
  * [**APEX Accelerator**](https://business.utah.gov/apex/) helps small businesses secure [government contracts](https://startup.utah.gov/secure-government-contracts-with-the-help-of-utahs-apex-accelerator/) through counseling, networking, and bid preparation. This program has facilitated over a billion dollars in federal procurement funding annually.
  * The [**Utah Small Business Credit Initiative**](https://business.utah.gov/usbci/) (USBCI), funded by the U.S. Treasury, enhances access to capital, particularly for underserved entrepreneurs. By partnering with banks and other lenders, the program allows flexible loan options, covering up to 50% of loans and blending its low-interest capital with standard loan rates.
  * The****[**Get Started: Business Idea Challenge**](https://startup.utah.gov/get-started/), launching in February 2025, is a monthly pitch competition hosted by the Startup State Initiative in partnership with the [Lassonde Entrepreneur Institute](https://lassonde.utah.edu/). With awards up to $500, founders can start or advance their businesses with short-term milestones.

### **Crowdfunding**

Since the early 2010s, [crowdfunding](https://startup.utah.gov/crowdfunding-a-democratized-way-to-raise-capital/) has become an increasingly viable way for a business to raise capital without relying on traditional lenders by pooling small contributions from many individuals online. It also helps to validate ideas and build community support. Successful campaigns set clear goals, maintain transparency, and often offer rewards such as early product access. Platforms like [Kickstarter](https://www.kickstarter.com/), [GoFundMe](https://www.gofundme.com/), and [Patreon](https://www.patreon.com/) cater to different niches, so it’s important to figure out which best suits the startup’s needs. Many Utah businesses, such as [Thread](https://startup.utah.gov/revolutionizing-wallets-how-thread-wove-personality-into-practicality/), have leveraged this democratized source of funding. 

### **Venture Capital and Angel Investors**

Venture capital is a form of private investment commonly associated with tech and high-growth startups. VC firms pool funds from multiple investors and provide funding in exchange for equity, assuming significant risk but with the potential for substantial returns. Benefits often include mentorship and industry connections. 

[Angel investors](https://startup.utah.gov/utah-angel-investor-groups-fuel-startup-growth-across-the-state/) operate similarly but invest personal funds rather than pooled capital, focusing on early-stage startups. Utah’s [Park City Angels](http://parkcityangels.com/) and [Salt Lake City Angels](http://slcangels.org/) are among the leading angel investment groups fueling the state’s startup ecosystem.

### **Bootstrapping**

Bootstrapping, which entails funding a business using personal savings, early revenues, and careful cost management, is often the most straightforward way to start a business. While growth may take longer without external investment, it allows founders to retain full control and avoid debt or investor obligations. Companies like [Consolve](https://startup.utah.gov/consolve-empowers-startups-to-grow-faster-smarter-and-with-confidence/) and Utah’s [Meat and Food Co-op](https://startup.utah.gov/food-and-meat-co-op-turning-a-family-necessity-into-a-thriving-community/) have successfully reinvested profits to expand their operations.

### **Conclusion**

As there are many ways to fund a startup, it is essential to research and assess the business’s needs before committing to a source of financing. In many cases, combining multiple funding sources may be the key to achieving profitability, allowing companies to choose options that best align with their goals.

title: Bolstering Your Business With Intellectual Property
description: This guide teaches business owners how to identify, protect, and secure intellectual property—patents, trademarks, copyrights, and trade secrets—to safeguard competitive advantage. It covers IP types, registration steps via USPTO and state resources, and Utah-specific support for entrepreneurs seeking affordable or free IP assistance.
body:
As a business owner, safeguarding your intellectual property is an important step for long-term success. Intellectual property includes the rights to creative ideas or inventions turned into something tangible — patents protect inventions, trademarks safeguard your brand, and copyrights cover creative works like designs and written content. Trade secrets, while unregistered, are critical to many businesses. Each of these contributes to your business’s unique value, which you want to keep safe from being copied or used without permission.

#### **Identify Your Intellectual Property**

The first step is identifying the[ type of IP protection](https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks/basics/trademark-patent-copyright) your business needs. Resources like the United States Patent and Trademark Office’s[ IP Identifier Tool](https://ipidentifier.uspto.gov/) and[ Patent and Trademark Resource Centers](https://www.uspto.gov/about-us/uspto-office-locations/utah) can help determine which of the following protections best fits your situation:

  * [Patent](https://www.uspto.gov/patents): legal rights granting an inventor control over how their new invention is made, used, or sold for a certain period of time.

  * [Copyright](https://www.copyright.gov/what-is-copyright/): legal protection giving creators the exclusive right to control how their original works, like books, music, or movies, are used or shared.

  * [Trademark](https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks): a registered symbol, word, phrase, or design that distinguishes and identifies the source of goods or services, helping to safeguard your brand from misuse.

  * [Trade secret](https://www.uspto.gov/ip-policy/trade-secret-policy): confidential information, like formulas, processes, or strategies, that gives a competitive advantage to a business and is protected by keeping it private.

#### **Secure Intellectual Property Rights**

Once identified, secure your IP rights. Resources like the[ United States Patent and Trademark Office](https://www.uspto.gov),[ the U.S. Copyright Office](https://www.copyright.gov), and the Utah Department of Commerce’s[ Utah Trademark](https://corporations.utah.gov/business-entities/trademark/) offer state and federal IP registration options.

If you plan to operate globally, remember that IP protection is region-specific. Organizations, including the[ World Intellectual Property Organization](https://www.wipo.int), provide guidance on international IP policies and best practices.

#### **Utah Resources for Entrepreneurs**

Utah entrepreneurs can leverage resources like the[ USPTO Rocky Mountain Regional Outreach Office](https://www.uspto.gov/about-us/uspto-locations/rocky-mountain) or[ Mi Casa Resource Center](https://micasaresourcecenter.org/probopat/) for affordable or free IP assistance. Local Patent and Trademark Resource Centers, such as those at the[ University of Utah](https://campusguides.lib.utah.edu/patents/ptrc) and[ Utah Tech University](https://utahtech.libguides.com/patents), are valuable resources offering IP guidance tailored to Utah entrepreneurs.

Protecting your intellectual property may be a strategic investment and necessity for your company’s growth. By utilizing resources and taking proactive steps, you can safeguard your ideas, strengthen your brand, and ensure your business remains relevant in a competitive market.

title: Five Ways to Build a Strong Network as a Utah Entrepreneur
description: This guide teaches Utah entrepreneurs five practical strategies to build a strong business network: joining local chambers and industry organizations, attending expos and meetups, leveraging incubators and accelerators, finding mentors, and connecting with emerging talent. It serves early-stage founders seeking partnerships, funding opportunities, and industry insights through community involvement and relationship-building.
body:
Building a robust business network is key to your startup thriving in today’s business environment. A well-developed network — connections with professionals and organizations — opens doors to valuable partnerships, industry insights, funding opportunities, and more to boost your business.

Here are five ways to establish and grow your network:

**1\. Join local business organizations**

Join your [local chamber of commerce](https://utahassociationofchambers.com/directory/) to access networking opportunities, resources for business growth, and events to connect you with other professionals.

Identify industry-specific organizations to connect with like-minded professionals and stay informed on market trends. Organizations such as BioHive, Silicon Slopes, Women Tech Council, 47G Utah Aerospace and Defense, and others offer tailored resources and access to industry influencers to help expand your reach.

**2\. Attend networking events**

Utah is home to numerous business expos and conferences including the [One Utah Summit](https://oneutahsummit.utah.gov/) and [Silicon Slopes Summit](https://www.siliconslopes.com/summit) where attendees network while gaining professional development.

Smaller meetups and workshops focus on connecting entrepreneurs face-to-face. Entrepreneur networking events like [1 Million Cups](https://www.1millioncups.com/s/) allow you to hear from other startups and share your expertise. 

**3\. Leverage incubators and accelerators**

Utah’s business incubators and accelerators — such as [RevRoad](https://revroad.com/), [Kinect Capital](https://kinectcapital.org/), or [iHub](https://www.ihubutah.org/) — support early-stage companies with mentorship, resources, and networking to help startups rapidly grow and succeed. Joining a business incubator or accelerator allows you to rub shoulders with other entrepreneurs while building beneficial skills.

**4\. Find local mentors**

Successful business mentors provide startups with valuable guidance and insights from real-world experience, helping them navigate challenges and avoid common pitfalls. Seasoned leaders can offer strategic advice, introduce key connections, and provide support to accelerate your company’s growth and increase its chances of long-term success.

**5\. Connect with new talent**

Engage with Utah’s emerging entrepreneur space by connecting with young talent through volunteering as a guest speaker at startup events or mentor at business incubators, university career centers, and public networking events. Building relationships with fresh talent can provide valuable insights into innovative and emerging markets and an opportunity to tap into the latest education and skills.

Through strategic networking, community involvement, and relationship-building, you can strengthen your business network and take your business to the next level.Go to [startup.utah.gov/resources](http://startup.utah.gov/resources) to find more resources to grow your network.

title: Networking: How Events Bolster Your Business and Grow Community
description: This guide teaches Utah entrepreneurs how to leverage networking events and community gatherings to build relationships, attract investors, and grow their businesses. It profiles key Utah events—One Utah Summit, 1 Million Cups, Silicon Slopes Summit, Third Thursday @ Three, and Utah Tech Week—showing how each creates opportunities for pitching, feedback, and meaningful connections. Ideal for founders at any stage seeking to expand their network and accelerate momentum.
body:
Effective networking is one of the most powerful tools an entrepreneur can have. Whether building support from fellow entrepreneurs, attracting investors, or connecting with customers, a strong network can be the difference between momentum and stagnation.

Fortunately for Utah’s founders, the state offers a wide array of groups, gatherings, and events to help foster these vital connections. From weekly meetups to annual conferences, here are some great resources to grow your entrepreneurial network.

[**One Utah Summit**](https://oneutahsummit.utah.gov/)**** brings together leaders from the government, local businesses, and the broader community to advance economic opportunity across the state. Held each fall, the summit features keynote speakers, industry panels, and networking sessions tailored to Utah’s entrepreneurs and changemakers. With a strong focus on innovation, collaboration, and statewide impact, it offers a unique space to share ideas, explore solutions, and connect with those shaping Utah’s future.

[**1 Million Cups**](https://startup.utah.gov/unlock-connections-and-ideas-at-orems-1-million-cups/) is a weekly gathering that helps entrepreneurs pitch ideas, get feedback, and connect with peers. Held every Wednesday morning, the meetings begin with brief introductions, followed by two entrepreneur pitches and open networking to foster building relationships. Whether sharing a new venture or simply showing up to support and learn, each session provides opportunities to make meaningful connections.

[**Silicon Slopes Summit**](https://startup.utah.gov/silicon-slopes-empowering-startups-and-fueling-innovation/) is one of the state’s largest gatherings for entrepreneurs, innovators, and tech leaders. With thousands of attendees and high-profile speakers, it offers opportunities to share ideas, learn from top companies, and build professional relationships. Events like Startup Alley allow emerging founders to showcase ventures and even meet investors, helping them take the next big step.

[**Third Thursday @ Three**](https://startup.utah.gov/third-thursday-three-is-where-and-when-to-pitch-your-startup/) is a monthly event for entrepreneurs, investors, and startup enthusiasts. Hosted at Kiln Lehi, it features five fast-paced startup pitches followed by open networking, making it a great place to find potential collaborators, mentors, or investors. Whether sharing an idea or exploring the scene, Third Thursday @ Three connects you with Utah’s vibrant and growing startup ecosystem.

[**Utah Tech Week**](https://startup.utah.gov/celebrate-utahs-thriving-tech-scene-at-utah-tech-week/) is a prime opportunity for founders, investors, and professionals to grow their networks within Utah and celebrate its thriving tech scene. The annual event features dozens of independently hosted panels, workshops, and gatherings, each designed to spark collaboration and “happy collisions” among attendees. Highlights include a high-stakes pitch competition and the Night Market, where local vendors and the community will come together to connect, celebrate, and grow.

These are just a few of Utah’s many events and gatherings that help to build community and foster connections. To find other offerings, visit the Startup State Initiative’s [resource page](https://startup.utah.gov/resources/), or learn how to [start your business](https://startup.utah.gov/entrepreneur-journey/) in Utah.

title: Networking: What Local Coworking Spaces Are Offering Your Startup
description: This guide teaches Utah founders how to leverage local coworking spaces and business incubators to build networks and access resources. It profiles Kiln, iHub, and The Mill—spaces offering flexible workspaces, mentorship, investor connections, and events—plus rural alternatives like chambers of commerce. Ideal for early-stage founders seeking collaboration, peer support, and pathways to funding.
body:
In business, networking isn’t just a tool — it’s a necessity. Whether it’s gathering support from fellow entrepreneurs, fiscal backing from investors, or a devoted customer base, growing your network can be the key to success.

Fortunately for Utah’s founders, the state offers a wide range of coworking hubs and business incubators that provide both resources to grow and opportunities to connect. With varying amenities and locations, here are a few standout spaces where startups can thrive.

[Kiln](https://startup.utah.gov/more-than-an-office-how-kiln-elevates-work-and-well-being/) is a leading coworking environment in Utah, offering startups a place to grow alongside like-minded innovators. With dozens of amenity-rich locations across the western U.S., Kiln’s flexible workspaces foster collaboration, creativity, and connection. Members can tap into a broad network of peers, mentors, and industry experts — what Kiln calls “a living library” for fast problem-solving. Its dynamic event calendar includes pitch nights, networking socials, wellness classes, and investor meetups, helping founders form meaningful relationships and build lasting professional connections.

[iHub](https://startup.utah.gov/ihub-utah-empowering-the-next-generation-of-entrepreneurs/) is more than a workspace — it’s a collaborative community where early-stage founders grow their networks and accelerate their ventures. Entrepreneurs work alongside experienced mentors and fellow business leaders, gaining hands-on support in areas like fundraising, legal strategy, and business development. With access to free office space, capital resources, and regular networking events, iHub fosters peer support and long-term growth.

[The Mill](https://startup.utah.gov/growing-utahs-next-generation-of-businesses-at-the-mill/) at Salt Lake Community College serves as a powerful networking hub and incubator, offering 24/7 access to coworking areas, private offices, and shared amenities. Startups can benefit from workshops and events designed to connect them with advisors, investors, and collaborators. On-site programs like the [Salt Lake SBDC](https://themillatslcc.com/resource/small-business-development-center/) and [Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses](https://themillatslcc.com/education/goldman-sachs-10000-small-businesses/) add even more support for companies ready to grow.

These are just a few of the many coworking options available across Utah. For those in more [rural environments](https://startup.utah.gov/how-a-statewide-coalition-is-fueling-entrepreneurship-in-rural-utah/), local [chambers of commerce](https://startup.utah.gov/how-local-chambers-help-small-businesses-thrive-in-utah/) help fill in the gap, offering not only workspaces — such as [San Juan’s business hubs](https://startup.utah.gov/san-juan-chambers-revival-marks-a-turning-point-in-rural-utah/) — but also serve as valuable connectors to help grow founder networks.

Looking for additional resources to help grow your network and strengthen your business? Visit the Startup State Initiative’s [resource page](https://startup.utah.gov/resources/) to discover additional tools, programs, and communities, or learn how to [start your business](https://startup.utah.gov/entrepreneur-journey/) in Utah.

title: Ready To Go Global? What Entrepreneurs Should Consider About International Expansion
description: This guide teaches entrepreneurs how to evaluate and prepare for international expansion by considering four key factors: comprehensive business planning, cultural and market differences, strategic partnerships, and financing. It serves Utah-based founders considering global markets and highlights state resources like World Trade Center Utah's readiness checks and STEP grants. Includes real examples of successful trade missions generating $193M+ in opportunities.
body:
Utah has long been known as a new frontier for innovation and its culture of international connectivity. Global expansion can lead to growth for many startups and entrepreneurs, with access to broader markets, a wider workforce, and increased brand recognition.

The trade missions partnered with the [Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity](https://business.utah.gov/international/) and [World Trade Center Utah](https://www.wtcutah.com/) in 2023 are a prime example of the state’s global reach, where 41 Utah-based companies traveled to France, the United Kingdom, and Mexico. Over 200 business meetings opened $193.25 million in new trade opportunities for Utah.

A [recent trade mission](https://business.utah.gov/news/utah-trade-delegation-travels-to-republic-of-korea-and-japan-to-forge-economic-ties/) allowed 21 Utah companies to forge connections in a different part of the globe — South Korea and Japan. The exchange strengthened Utah’s established ties with these countries, anticipating positive results.

However, taking your business global isn’t a one-size-fits-all strategy. Understanding diverse markets, potential challenges, and cultural differences is crucial to evaluating your business if global expansion aligns with your strategy.

Here are four considerations for going global:

  1. **Comprehensive Business Plan**

A clear plan is essential for navigating the complexities of starting a business, particularly in international markets. Outline your growth strategy with goals, milestones, and resources needed to sustain expansion abroad. Consider clear and realistic timelines, budgets, and performance metrics.

  2. **Cultural and Market Differences**

Global expansion requires learning new consumer behaviors, legal and political systems, and business practices. Market research is pivotal. It may be necessary to tailor products, services, and messaging for each market.

  3. **Strategic Partnerships**

Strong global partnerships can equal success when entering new markets. Experienced distributors, consultants, or partners can help identify and mitigate international challenges. These relationships can bridge gaps in language, market understanding, and operational logistics.

  4. **Financing and Financial Risks**

As with starting any business, global expansion requires capital. Evaluate your financial readiness and explore reliable financing and government-backed programs. Be aware of potential issues with currency fluctuations, payment schedules, or regulatory challenges.

If you believe going international is right for your company, consider seeking business and legal advisors. [World Trade Center Utah](https://www.wtcutah.com/) offers valuable, no-cost readiness checks and market research assistance to successfully expand internationally, in addition to its [State Trade Expansion Program (STEP) grant](https://www.wtcutah.com/grants). It’s vital to assess your resources, readiness, and ability to adapt to diverse markets before making the leap.

With [75% of the world’s purchasing power](https://www.wtcutah.com/market-expansion#:~:text=With%2075%25%20of%20the%20world%E2%80%99s%20purchasing%20power%20outside%20of%20the%20U.S.) located outside of the U.S., is it time for your company to capitalize on going global?

The information in this article is current as of the publishing date and is intended for informational purposes only. This article does not, and is not intended to, constitute legal, tax, or business advice. Any resources and organizations mentioned, unless an entity of or a partner of the state of Utah, are not formally endorsed by the Startup State Initiative or state of Utah.

title: Six Things to Include in Your Pitch Deck
description: Learn the six essential components of a compelling pitch deck: CEO background, problem identification, solution presentation, business model, traction/growth metrics, and funding ask. This guide teaches entrepreneurs how to structure pitches that convince investors by leading with founder expertise, data-backed problems, visual solutions, clear monetization, proven traction, and specific funding requests with milestone plans.
body:
Creating a compelling pitch deck is crucial for any entrepreneur aiming to raise funds and grow their business. Here are six things to include in your pitch deck.

1\. Background of the CEO/Presenter

Show how your expertise (from personal experience or deep industry knowledge) makes you fit to solve the problem. How did you discover the problem you aim to solve? For instance, “I have been in supply chain management for 10 years. I noticed the following problems with current solutions 1… 2… 3…”

2\. The Problem

Identify the market issue potential buyers face. Emphasize with data the pain points and how existing solutions are inadequate. For example, “I have many streaming subscriptions but struggled to find a specific movie. Studies show 45% of consumers spend over 15 minutes searching for specific content across an average of 4 streaming subscriptions per household.” (Data is for illustrative purposes only.) For investors to care about your solution, first help them understand the problem.

3\. The Solution

After establishing the problem, present your solution. Show (don’t tell) how your product or service directly addresses the issues. Use visuals such as images of an app or prototype. Mirror the problem slide to address resolutions to each pain point.

4\. Business Model

Explain how you make money through subscription fees, product sales, or services. For example, “It costs $0.60 to manufacture the product, and we sell it for $15. With a repeat business model, replacement products are sold every other year.” If you’re still figuring out the pricing model, mention that you’re testing various models.

5\. Traction and Growth

Showcase your milestones, such as customer acquisitions, partnerships, or sales growth. Present logos of current recognizable clients, funding received, or news and awards. Illustrate what you can accomplish with the desired funding. Don’t be humble about your ability to execute!

6\. The Ask

Conclude with a clear funding request and how it will be used to hit your next milestones. “We’re seeking $1 million to expand our team and accelerate product development.” You should spend most of your time on this slide as investors will examine it in detail.

With this structure, your pitch deck can effectively communicate your goals and give investors the confidence to invest in your vision.

title: Turning Your Passion Into a Successful Business Idea
description: This guide teaches how to validate a business idea by identifying passions, researching market demand, defining value propositions, and testing with real customers. It serves aspiring entrepreneurs exploring whether their concept can succeed. Covers four key steps: list passions, analyze the market for gaps, clarify what sets your solution apart, and prototype with customer feedback. References free SBDC consulting and SBA resources.
body:
The foundation of any successful business starts with a great idea. Passions, skills, or addressing your own frustrations can inspire the idea. But how do you know if your idea has the potential to succeed?

The [Utah Small Business Development Center](https://utahsbdc.org/) (SBDC) offers free, personalized business consulting. The consultants can guide you through the process and help you navigate the complexities of starting a business. 

The [Small Business Administration](https://www.sba.gov/blog/startup-business-ideas-4-steps-identify-right-one) (SBA) also suggests some steps to help determine which business idea is most likely to succeed: 

  1. **Identify your passions:** Start by making a list of your passions. Then, write complete sentences explaining what you commit to doing with each passion. Think about things you love to do that may have solved problems or addressed challenges you’ve had. 
  2. **Research the market:** Conduct research to see if people are willing to buy your solution. Write a list of potential situations where your idea would be beneficial. Spend some time online to see what is currently available. Analyze similar products to identify gaps in the marketplace that your business could fill.
  3. **Define your value proposition:** Your value proposition is what sets your product or service apart from other products. Does your product or service solve a problem, and would people be willing to pay for a solution? Creating a clear value proposition and target market allows you to explain your product’s key benefits.
  4. **Test your idea:** Start testing your product or service with real customers. Create a prototype so you can see how they react. If you receive positive feedback, you can continue launching your idea. Otherwise, you may need to make adjustments before moving forward. Collect positive and negative feedback to determine what tweaks to make.

For those who don’t have a unique idea but still want to start a business, the [Small Business Administration](https://www.sba.gov/blog/8-easy-businesses-start) offers several business ideas. They suggest exploring ideas spanning from creative fields such as a logo designer, photographer, or video creator; practical solutions such as a house and pet sitter, errand service, or tutor; or remote work such as an e-commerce seller or virtual assistant.

Starting a new business is an exciting journey! Before you begin, think through your idea and make sure it has the potential to be successful, look into what solutions are currently available, and check with state and local authorities for the necessary licenses and permits.

title: Business Elevated Podcast Showcases Utah’s Thriving Entrepreneurial Scene
description: Business Elevated Podcast, launched by Utah's Governor's Office of Economic Opportunity in 2019, showcases entrepreneurs and business leaders shaping Utah's economy. With 200+ episodes, it features interviews with executives, community leaders, and innovators discussing their experiences and insights. The guide teaches aspiring podcasters to define clear objectives, know their audience, secure proper equipment, and choose the right syndication platform for distribution across Apple Podcasts and Spotify.
body:
Since its official launch in early 2019, the Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity’s [Business Elevated Podcast](https://business.utah.gov/category/podcast/) has provided a platform for entrepreneurs, executives, and community leaders to share their experiences of living and working in Utah.

Initiated in 2018 under the leadership of Val Hale, former [GOEO](https://business.utah.gov/) executive director, and Pete Codella, current managing director of business services, the podcast highlights the state’s flourishing entrepreneurial ecosystem and addresses common misconceptions.

Over the years, Business Elevated has become a prominent voice for Utah’s business community. Initially held in person, interviews shifted online during the COVID-19 pandemic. While the podcast primarily features Utah-based executives, it has also included business leaders from as far as London who have professional ties to the state.

With over 200 episodes, many notable figures have appeared, including Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson and First Lady Abby Cox. For Codella, one standout episode included a conversation with [Cotopaxi’s Davis Smith](https://business.utah.gov/podcast/cotopaxi-responsibility-and-sustainability/), during which he shared stories of his passion for survival challenges.

Another highlight for Codella was a conversation he shared with the founder of [Auticon](https://auticon.com/), a service that helps [place individuals with autism](https://business.utah.gov/podcast/podcast-vance-checketts-integrating-neurodiversity-into-tech/) in roles that match their technical skills, something that hit close to home as his wife teaches special education at a local high school.

“In that episode, it was amazing to see a pathway for many families and individuals to build independent, productive lives and jobs,” Codella said. “It’s been a privilege to host incredible conversations and people throughout the years.”

Maintaining consistency has been key to the podcast’s success. New episodes are released weekly, with Codella acting as the primary host. The podcast is syndicated through [Libsyn](https://libsyn.com/), allowing distribution across major platforms like [Apple Podcasts](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/business-elevated/id1453052684) and [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2kqzVlVfsXk9JSj82KUKHT).

For aspiring podcasters, Codella advises having a clear objective and knowing the target audience, which informs best practices for conducting interviews, as well as obtaining the proper equipment and selecting the right syndication platform.

As the Business Elevated Podcast continues to produce content, its team welcomes feedback and episode suggestions, which can be done by emailing [business@utah.gov](mailto:business@utah.gov). The podcast remains committed to showcasing the diverse voices contributing to Utah’s dynamic economic landscape and telling the stories of the people living and working in this great state.
